newsitem.title: USA: Amex posts higher profits, announces major job cuts.
newsitem.headline: Amex posts higher profits, announces major job cuts.

text.p: American Express Co., reporting higher-than-expected fourth quarter earnings, said Monday it would cut 3,300 jobs from a worldwide work force of about 72,000 as part of a reorganization of its Travel Related Services unit.
About 2,000 of the job cuts will be made overseas and some facilities will be consolidated, American Express said.
Travel Related Services has some 60,000 employees.

Spokeswoman Susan Miller said some of the employees who will be affected by the restructuring have been alerted but for others details were still being worked out. She said the 3,300 figure represented both job eliminations and the number of people being let go.
Regarding the facilities to be consolidated, she said "they are not the major locations."
American Express, a major travel, financial and network services provider, had fourth quarter earnings of $595 million, or $1.23 a share. A year earlier it earned $384 million, or 77 cents a share.
A consensus of earnings estimates by First Call Inc. put American Express' fourth quarter earnings at 89 cents a share.
Revenues rose to $4.26 billion from $4.05 billion.

Asked about the amount of cost savings expected in the future, Miller said the restructuring steps were "part of our ongoing re-engineering initiatives which are designed to reduce our cost base so that we reinvest those savings into growth areas of the business."
The company has previously defined growth areas as international, financial services and its card network.
For all of 1996, American Express earned $1.9 billion, or $3.90 a share, compared with $1.6 billion, or $3.11 a share a year earlier.
Revenues rose to $16.2 billion from $15.8 billion in 1995.
Earnings for 1996 include a $300 million gain on an exchange of stock and a charge of $138 million for restructuring.

American Express' travel related services unit had 1996 operating income of $1.23 billion, up 13 percent from 1995, reflecting higher worldwide billing on American Experess Cards and growth in Cardmember loans outstanding.

American Express Financial Advisors had earnings of $594 million, up 18 percent from 1995, aided by increased revenues from managed assets and growth in distribution feed primarily from sales of mutual funds.
Record sales were reported for mutual funds and life and other insurance products. Sales of annuities increased over 1995, while sales of investment certificates decreased.
American Express Bank had 1996 net income of $68 million, a 12 percent decrease over 1995. The decline reflected lower revenues and a higher provision for loan losses.
American Express stock closed down $1.625 at $59.50 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.

Moshe Orenbuch, analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein Co., said the dip in the stock price might have reflected disappointment on the part of some investors that the cost savings in the restructuring would not flow to the bottom line but instead would be reinvested in the business.

He said while growth has improved for American Express in the last two quarters the company was still wrestling with expenses. Asked if reinvesting the money was a good move for American Epxress, he said, "it's certainly the right thing to do and it's consistent with their attitude in the past."
